The estimate is +0.025 passage-rate units. A bootstrap (4000 resamples within genre-by-period cells) gives a 95% CI of [0.003, 0.046]. An OLS model adjusting for genre, origin, date_confidence, log editions and log author productivity, with standard errors clustered by author, gives +0.026 [0.001, 0.050]. Composition checks: origin shares are stable across periods. Mean editions fall slightly (1.26 early vs 1.06 late), and author productivity is similar. Date_confidence is unbalanced: 34% of early works are high-confidence versus 48% of late works. The overall result is only just significant, and it is driven by the less reliably dated works. Within high-confidence works only, the effect is +0.015 with CI [-0.029, 0.055]. Medium-confidence works give +0.022 [-0.015, 0.056]. Low-confidence works give +0.043 [0.005, 0.075]. The sign is consistent across origins and among single-edition works (+0.02 to +0.03). Moving the cutoff to 1856 or 1866 gives +0.03 or +0.015. Decade means are noisy because pre-1850 counts are tiny. Other possible explanations: dating error that clusters late-assigned works with travel content, genre-mix and selection differences in which early works survived into the corpus, and noise from single-passage binary rates. The cited passage IDs are examples coded as DISTANCE_TRAVEL in both periods. They show what the construct looks like but cannot establish a trend. A small increase is plausible, but it does not survive restriction to well-dated works, so the evidence does not support claiming a robust historical shift."
